## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard first-strand cyclotomic quotient with right append, the
generic categorification $\gamma$ and the vacuum-normalized integral
isomorphism $\phi$, in the geometric parameter scope above.

[F1] The generic negative-half global basis and its projection
([[thm-self-dual-indecomposable-klr-projectives-give-the-negative-half-lower-global-basis]],
[[thm-global-basis-projection-from-the-negative-half-to-a-highest-weight-module]],
[[thm-klr-categorification-of-the-negative-quantum-half]]).

[F2] The word-mirror involution and the quantum star
([[lem-word-mirror-involution-of-a-klr-algebra-and-the-quantum-star]]): it
commutes with projective Hom duality, reverses separated-block induction, and
induces the multiplication-reversing star fixing every $F_i$ and $q$.

[F3] The cover-descent and crystal-compatibility inputs
([[lem-cyclotomic-projective-covers-and-dualities-descend-through-the-quotient]],
[[lem-canonical-elementary-crystal-extraction-and-highest-weight-survivors]],
[[thm-simple-and-indecomposable-projective-crystals-agree-with-b-lambda]],
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-projective-k-zero-is-the-integral-highest-weight-module]]).

[F4] The positive FIRST-block coefficient-$1$ expansion and integral LEFT-string ideal equality of [[lem-klr-projective-duality-and-positive-divided-string-leading-terms]], and the FIRST/RIGHT one-step simple recursion of [[lem-klr-one-step-simple-restriction-induction-and-first-dot-index]]. These are the existing algebraic inputs to the approved FIRST/RIGHT comparison; the crystal graph on covers is transported from heads, not an independent linear action on a projective basis.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** compare the side conventions on divided words, use the
mirror twist to convert star into the identity, and read survival and
non-merging off the cover-descent lemma.

1.1 The raw extension map on divided words. Right append sends a word $\nu_1\cdots\nu_n$ to $F_{\nu_n}\cdots F_{\nu_1}v_\Lambda$, whereas the generic multiplication convention assigns $F_{\nu_1}\cdots F_{\nu_n}$; on actual divided word classes the map is therefore $\pi_\Lambda\circ*$. Their $A$-span is all generic $K_0$ by [F1], so this determines the map integrally, giving $\phi[q_\Lambda(P)]=\pi_\Lambda(*(\gamma^{-1}[P]))$; composing with the generic mirror twist of [F2], which supplies exactly $*$ and commutes with projective Hom duality, gives $\pi_\Lambda$ without star. [F1, F2]

1.2 Positive star on the global basis. The generic mirror equivalence of [F2] preserves indecomposability and commutes with projective Hom duality, hence permutes the normalized generic covers. Once the generic global theorem in [F1] is instantiated, their classes are exactly the positive lower global vectors. Its induced quantum star therefore permutes these vectors with positive sign: $*G^-(b)=G^-(b^*)$. This is a consequence of the generic global theorem used here, not an input to its geometric or sign proof. [F1, F2]

2.1 Survival and non-merging. For a surviving normalized generic simple $S$, quotient Hom base change in the cover-descent lemma [F3] sends its normalized projective cover to the cyclotomic normalized cover, commutes with $\#$, and preserves its unscaled head pairing; if its simple is killed, the quotient is zero, because any nonzero finite quotient of the cover has a simple head and adjunction would produce a surviving generic head of the original cover. Thus raw extension of a generic normalized indecomposable projective is zero or a single normalized indecomposable cyclotomic projective, and distinct surviving heads do not merge; the image is $\pi_\Lambda G^-(b^*)$ respectively $G^-_\Lambda(\pi_\Lambda b^*)$ under the projections of [F1]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F3]

3.1 RIGHT-simple labels. The FIRST-block coefficient-$1$ expansion and LEFT-string ideal equality of [F4] identify the maximal FIRST-block partition of each generic cover with the adapted LEFT-string partition of its lower global vector. The one-step simple recursion increases this FIRST-string position by one; the adapted quantum recursion does the same. Induction on lowering paths from the vacuum therefore identifies the FIRST-end simple label with the ordinary canonical label. The mirror equivalence exchanges FIRST and RIGHT head/socle shift orbits, fixes the vacuum and induces star on the normalized cover class, so in the canonical RIGHT-simple label $c$ the equality is $\gamma^{-1}[P(S_c)]=G^-(c^*)$. The raw extension formula of step 1.1 cancels the two stars and sends it to $G^-_\Lambda(\pi_\Lambda c)$, with exactly the survivor label of [F3]. Every normalized cyclotomic cover is obtained because every cyclotomic simple inflates to a generic simple whose cover descends. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the generic global-basis and quantum-projection contracts of [F1] and the canonical-extraction supplier of [F3]; no other step uses infinite choice. The claim concerns indecomposable projectives, not every finite projective quotient. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4] ∎

## Proof

**Proof technique:** map each normalized cyclotomic cover to its based-quotient

lifting lower global vectors through the generic theorem.

1.1 Cover classes land on lower global vectors. By [F1] all normalized cyclotomic covers are precisely the nonzero extensions of normalized generic covers, with distinct surviving simple heads; the based-quotient lemma sends each such class to a single positive lower global vector of $V_A(\Lambda)$, with no grading ambiguity because Hom base change preserves the $\#$-normalization and the degree-zero head pairing. Conversely the quantum global projection theorem [F2] supplies a generic global vector lifting every lower global vector of $V_A(\Lambda)$, and the generic theorem supplies its normalized generic cover; mirroring if necessary to use the raw first/right convention, its extension has that nonzero class and is a normalized indecomposable cover. Hence the assignment is surjective onto the lower basis. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Bijectivity and labels. The integral $K_0$ isomorphism and its free normalized projective basis make the assignment injective; the RIGHT crystal label identification of [F3] shows that the projective with RIGHT label $c\in B(\Lambda)$ maps to $G^-_\Lambda(c)$, with the FIRST/RIGHT label cancellation proved in the based-quotient lemma. The uniqueness is at the level of normalized indecomposable projective isomorphism classes, not of generic lifts, and no arbitrary-parameter based extension is asserted. before.statement: In exactly the symmetric normalized-$d_i=1$, characteristic-zero, loopless arbitrary-multiedge geometric-parameter regime of the lower projective theorem, the CANONICAL restricted-dual identification $\Psi_{\rm can}:G_0(R^\Lambda)\to V_A(\Lambda)^\vee$ maps normalized $D_\psi$-self-dual simple classes bijectively to the upper global basis, form-dual to the lower projective basis under the actual highest-weight contravariant form. A simple and its normalized projective COVER have the same $B(\Lambda)$ label; this is the cover/simple correspondence, not projective Hom duality applied to a simple. Canonical $G_0$ operators have the same projective normalization. The alternative KK module action remains valid, but its intertwiner is $\Psi_{\rm KK}=q^{\operatorname{def}_\Lambda(\beta)}\Psi_{\rm can}$ on root $\beta$ and sends a simple to that defect-rescaled upper vector. The unrescaled upper-basis claim is made only for $\Psi_{\rm can}$.
before.strategy:
1. The quotient-cover supplier gives $T(P(S),S')=\delta_{S,S'}$ in the normalized bases. By the lower theorem $\phi(P(S))$ is the lower global vector with the same crystal label. Therefore the functional $\Psi_{\rm can}(S)$ is exactly the weightwise dual lower-basis functional.
2. The integral projective theorem identifies tensor form on projectives with the actual highest-weight contravariant form. The upper/lower duality supplier identifies these restricted dual functionals with the upper global vectors and preserves crystal labels. This proves bijection and all normalization statements; neither generic negative-half form nor a vector-dual trace shift is substituted.
3. The $G_0$ theorem proves the canonical action and its defect-rescaled KK version. Keeping their two maps distinct preserves both sound quantum actions and the rank-one $\lambda=2$ check. The simple/projective crystal theorem supplies the same RIGHT labels independently. No based assertion is extended beyond the approved geometric scope.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The geometric-parameter regime of the lower projective theorem, the
normalized $D_\psi$-self-dual simples and normalized covers, and the two
restricted-dual identifications.

[F1] The quotient-cover pairing
([[lem-cyclotomic-projective-covers-and-dualities-descend-through-the-quotient]]):
$T(P(S),S')=\delta_{S,S'}$ in normalized bases.

[F2] The lower projective theorem
([[thm-self-dual-indecomposable-cyclotomic-klr-projectives-give-the-lower-global-basis]]):
$\phi(P(S))$ is the lower global vector with the same crystal label.

[F3] The integral projective and $G_0$ identifications
([[thm-cyclotomic-klr-projective-k-zero-is-the-integral-highest-weight-module]],
[[thm-cyclotomic-klr-module-g-zero-is-the-dual-integral-highest-weight-module]])
and the upper/lower duality and crystal compatibility
([[thm-upper-and-lower-global-bases-are-dual-and-crystal-compatible]],
[[def-upper-global-basis-by-the-contravariant-form]],
[[def-cyclotomic-klr-diagram-duality-and-graded-module-duals]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** pair the normalized simple functional against the lower
basis, identify it with the form-dual lower functional, and apply the
upper/lower duality theorem; then compare the two normalizations.

1.1 The functional $\Psi_{\mathrm{can}}(S)$. By [F1] the pairing is diagonal in normalized bases, and by [F2] the class $\phi(P(S))$ is the lower global vector with the same crystal label; therefore $\Psi_{\mathrm{can}}(S)$ is exactly the weightwise dual lower-basis functional with that label. [F1, F2]

2.1 Identification with the upper global basis. The integral projective identification [F3] identifies the tensor form on projectives with the actual highest-weight contravariant form; the upper/lower duality theorem identifies these restricted dual functionals with the upper global vectors and preserves crystal labels. This proves the bijection and the normalization statements, using neither a generic negative-half form nor a vector-dual trace shift. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 Cover/simple correspondence and the two actions. A simple and its normalized projective cover have the same $B(\Lambda)$ label by the cover/simple correspondence of [F2], not by applying projective Hom duality to a simple. The $G_0$ theorem [F3] proves the canonical action and its defect-rescaled KK version; keeping the two maps distinct preserves both sound quantum actions and the rank-one $\lambda=2$ check, with $\Psi_{\mathrm{KK}}=q^{\operatorname{def}_\Lambda(\beta)}\Psi_{\mathrm{can}}$ on root $\beta$, so that only $\Psi_{\mathrm{can}}$ gives the unrescaled upper-basis claim. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the QG-5 global-basis duality and the generic basis suppliers of [F2] and [F3]. [step 2.1, F2, F3] ∎

before.title: Multipartitions with fixed component cores are cyclotomic Jantzen-connected
before.statement: Under the arbitrary-field finite-e nondegenerate cyclotomic hypotheses of [[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]], any two $\ell$-multipartitions of a common rank $n$ with equal componentwise $e$-cores are $J$-equivalent, even if their component sizes differ. At fixed component sizes, the full-level coefficient for a change in a single component equals its level-one coefficient. The proof consumes the actual native21 same-e-core Hecke Specht-block theorem for all ranks, not its readiness receipt, and imports no Carter-partition classification.
before.strategy:
Fix the rank n and charges in the Statement. First suppose the component sizes agree. For a single component a of rank m, the actual level-one Hecke algebra is the finite Hecke algebra by [[prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras]]. Its same-core Specht-block clause [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], together with [[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]] at level one, connects any two rank-m partitions with equal core by level-one Jantzen edges. The Dipper–James to Murphy convention change is conjugate-dual; core equality is preserved because core(transpose λ)=transpose(core λ). Thus the exact existing clause applies over the original F without an algebraic-closure hypothesis. Rank m=0 has a single empty partition and needs no block theorem.

For two full multipartitions that differ only in component a, every contributing equal-remainder hook pair in J lies in a. The common residue factor Q_a t^(na) is a unit of O. Replacing it by the level-one factor Q_a t^m also multiplies each foot difference by a Laurent unit. Hence its valuation is unchanged, and the full-level J coefficient is exactly the level-one coefficient. Insert the level-one paths in a and leave the other components fixed. Changing the components one at a time connects all equal-size-component multipartitions with the same component cores.

If component weights differ, choose a component whose weight exceeds its target and one whose weight is deficient. A positive-weight component has a removable e-hook, by its core construction. Wrap an e-hook in the deficient component with the same foot residue: for any prescribed foot residue f, moving the lowest bead on runner f−1 down by e creates such a hook, since its foot residue is the starting beta position plus1. The changed components determine the removed/added hook pair uniquely. In the appropriate dominance orientation their J contribution is one signed valuation, with no cancellation. Equal foot residue means its nonzero generic difference is divisible by t−1, so the valuation is a positive integer. Nonzero generic foot differences are part of the exact J formula supplier [[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]]; no unit-difference or characteristic-zero restriction is inserted. Thus the transfer is a Jantzen edge. It lowers the sum of squares of discrepancies of component hook weights by at least2. Finitely many such transfers equalize component weights. The preceding fixed-size argument then completes the connection. Every moved e-hook preserves the component core, and all steps preserve total rank.

after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Jantzen linkage equivalence [F1], the exact $J$ formula [F2],
the level-one identification [F3], the same-core Hecke block theorem [F4],
and the $e$-core/e-weight conventions [F5]–[F7].

[F1] $\lambda\sim_J\mu$ iff the corresponding Schur standards share a block
iff the Murphy Specht modules share a Hecke block, at any level and over any
field in the stated regime
([[lem-cyclotomic-jantzen-equivalence-is-schur-and-hecke-block-linkage]]).

[F2] The integer $J_{\lambda\mu}$ is the signed sum of
$\nu_\pi(\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal O}(f_x^\lambda)-\operatorname{res}_{\mathcal O}(f_y^\mu))$
over equal-remainder equal-length hook pairs, $0$ unless $\lambda$ strictly
dominates $\mu$, and every foot difference is nonzero in $K$
([[thm-cyclotomic-schur-jantzen-sum-formula-from-rim-hook-valuations]]).

[F3] At level one the arbitrary-level cyclotomic Hecke algebra is the finite
type-A Hecke algebra
([[prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras]]).

[F4] Two type-A Hecke Specht modules are in the same block exactly when their
labels have the same $e$-core
([[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]).

[F5] $e$-core, $e$-quotient and $e$-weight of a partition
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]), with the core independent of the
removal order ([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]])
and the size/weight formula ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

[F6] The actual universal signed-conjugate comparison gives $P(\lambda^{\mathsf T})\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$, hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda^{\mathsf T})^\theta$; $\theta$ is an involutive algebra automorphism whose pullback is exact ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The rank $n$, the charges, and the suppliers of [F1]–[F5].

1.1 One component at a time, at level one. Suppose first that the component sizes agree. For a single component $a$ of rank $m$, the actual level-one Hecke algebra is the finite Hecke algebra by [F3]. Its same-core Specht-block clause [F4], together with the level-one case of the Jantzen linkage equivalence [F1], connects any two rank-$m$ partitions with equal $e$-core by level-one Jantzen edges. The exact signed-conjugate bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda^{\mathsf T})^\theta$, where $\theta(T_i)=-zT_i^{-1}$ and $P$ denotes the ordinary Dipper–James Specht module. If $\lambda,\mu$ have equal $e$-cores, their transposes have the equal transposed cores, so [F4] puts $P(\lambda^{\mathsf T})$ and $P(\mu^{\mathsf T})$ in the same ordinary Hecke block. An algebra automorphism sends primitive central idempotents bijectively to primitive central idempotents; its exact module pullback therefore preserves the equivalence of sharing a block. Applying the SAME $\theta$ to both modules gives the required Murphy block equality and then [F1] gives the level-one Jantzen connection. No untwisted conjugate-dual identity or algebraic-closure assumption is used. The rank $m=0$ case has a single empty partition and needs no block theorem. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6]

1.2 Equalizing the component weights. If the component weights differ, choose a component whose weight exceeds its target and one whose weight is deficient; a positive-weight component has a removable $e$-hook by its core construction [F5]. For any prescribed foot residue $f$, moving the lowest bead on runner $f-1$ down by $e$ creates an $e$-hook with that foot residue, since its foot residue is the starting beta position plus one; wrap this hook in the deficient component with the same foot residue. The changed components determine the removed and added hook pair uniquely, and in the appropriate dominance orientation their $J$ contribution is one signed valuation with no cancellation; equal foot residues mean the nonzero generic difference is divisible by $t-1$, so the valuation is a positive integer. Nonzero generic foot differences are part of the exact formula [F2], and no unit-difference or characteristic-zero restriction is inserted. Thus the transfer is a Jantzen edge; it lowers the sum of squares of the discrepancies of the component hook weights by at least $2$, so finitely many such transfers equalize the component weights. Every moved $e$-hook preserves its component's core by [F5], and every step preserves the total rank. [F2, F5]

2.1 Fixed component sizes. For two full multipartitions that differ only in component $a$, every contributing equal-remainder hook pair in $J$ lies in $a$: the other components are unchanged on both sides and cancelling hooks between two unchanged components would return the same multipartition. The common residue factor $Q_at^{na}$ is a unit of $\mathcal O$, and replacing it by the level-one factor $Q_at^m$ multiplies each foot difference by a Laurent unit, so the valuation is unchanged and the full-level $J$ coefficient equals the level-one coefficient of [F2]. Inserting the level-one paths of step 1.1 in component $a$ and leaving the other components fixed connects all multipartitions with equal component sizes and the same component cores. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.2 equalize component sizes along Jantzen edges from any starting multipartition, and step 2.1 connects all multipartitions of fixed component sizes with equal component cores. Composing the two finite chains connects any two multipartitions of rank $n$ with equal componentwise $e$-cores, proving that they are $J$-equivalent; the fixed-size comparison of coefficients is step 2.1. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Remarks

The lemma reduces the multipartition block question to the componentwise
$e$-core data and the level-one Hecke theorem, using the exact level-one to
finite-Hecke identification and the explicit hook transfer between
components. No choice principle is used: all chains and hook moves are
finite and explicitly constructed.

before.title: Weight-one block decomposition pattern
before.statement: Let $e\ge2$, let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, and put $n=m+e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy/dual-Specht) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this block satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$ for $1\le k<e$, so the decomposition matrix is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$; and exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]$ for $2\le k<e$ and $[S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]$, with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.
before.strategy: The abacus of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]] shows that the partitions of $n=m+e$ with $e$-core $\gamma$ are obtained from $\gamma$ by moving one bead up one row on one runner, so there are exactly $e$ of them; ordered by dominance they are $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$, with $\lambda_e$ the one whose bead has the lowest target position and $\lambda_1$ the one obtained by adjoining all $e$ boxes to the first row. For each $k$ the Jantzen sum formula of [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] evaluates in this weight-one configuration to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}_F(i)]\sim\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}_F]$, because the only nonzero hook valuations are the consecutive ones; the resulting triangular system, with the simple modules detected through [[lem-virtual-weyl-combinations-detect-q-schur-block-separation]] and the block classification, has the unique solution $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$ for $k<e$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. The $e$-restricted pattern follows from $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, which is exactly the non-$e$-restricted vanishing of the cell head, together with $F(W^{\lambda_1})=F(L^{\lambda_2})$ and the Schur-functor dictionary; the Dipper-James translation is the signed conjugate-cell dictionary with the same $\theta$ pullback on every Hecke module of the Specht-module definition. This is Mathas, Proposition 5.38 with its printed Jantzen computation, printed pp. 61-63; the numeric pattern is worked out again in this pair's examples companion. No choice principle is used.

after.title: The weight-one block decomposition pattern
after.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), let $\gamma$ be an $e$-core of $m$, and put $n=m+e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). There are exactly $e$ partitions $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$ of $n$ with $e$-core $\gamma$; list them in dominance order, $\lambda_1\rhd\lambda_2\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. In the source's (Murphy) normalisation the Weyl modules and simple modules of this weight-one class satisfy $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$ and $$[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]\qquad(1\le k<e),$$ so the decomposition matrix of the class is the $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix with rows and columns $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_e$. Moreover exactly $\lambda_1$ is not $e$-restricted, while $\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_e$ are. Under the Schur functor ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]) the corresponding Murphy Specht classes are $$[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}],\qquad [S^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_{k+1}}_{\mathrm M}]\ (2\le k<e),\qquad [S^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_e}_{\mathrm M}],$$ with $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$; conjugating partitions and applying the same $\theta$ pullback to both modules ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]) gives the corresponding decomposition matrix for the page's Dipper-James Specht modules in $e$-regular labels.

No choice principle is used.
after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, an $e$-core $\gamma$ of $m$, the integer $n=m+e$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,n)$ for $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, where $d\ge n$.

[F1] Each Weyl module has simple head $L^{\lambda}$ of multiplicity one, the decomposition matrix is dominance-unitriangular, and all simple modules are obtained this way ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). In a finite-dimensional module, a simple head implies indecomposability: any nonzero direct summand has a nonzero head, so two nonzero summands would give a nonsimple head.

[F2] The corrected balanced Jantzen formula sums positive filtration **submodules**, not their successive quotients: $$\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda}_F(i)]=\sum_{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda],\ b<c}\bigl(\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ab}]_{\hat q})-\nu_\pi([h^{\lambda}_{ac}]_{\hat q})\bigr)[W^{\beta+h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_b-h^{\lambda}_{ac}\varepsilon_c}_F].$$ Here $\beta_b=\lambda'_b+N-b$ for a fixed sufficiently long conjugate beta sequence, and the right hand symbols are alternating symbols: sort strictly decreasing, attach the sorting sign, and vanish on repeated or negative entries. The equal transfer preserves total size. Moreover $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$. This is the balanced hook-ratio formula required from [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Its source arithmetic must be repaired before binding: the manuscript's displayed beta indices are inconsistent, while its worked Example 5.28 determines the balanced transfer.

[F3] Core-quotient and abacus theory: a weight-one partition is obtained from a packed core abacus by moving the bottom bead of one runner down one place. The bead move removes/adds a rim $e$-hook, and distinct runners give distinct partitions ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Restricted means $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i$ ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F4] The exact Schur functor sends $W^{\lambda}$ to $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $L^{\lambda}$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$, whose nonzero labels are precisely the restricted partitions. The ordinary Specht dictionary uses conjugation and the same $\theta$ pullback on every module ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement. [F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q\ne1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}\ne0$, so $\nu([e]_X)=1$; also $\nu([h]_X)=0$ when $e\nmid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $\nu([e]_1)=\nu(p)=1$ and $\nu([h]_1)=0$ for $p\nmid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

before.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
before.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell$ the quantum characteristic of $q$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and
$n\ge r$. Let $S(n,r)$ be the type-A q-Schur algebra with the idempotent $e$
of the weight $(1^r)$, so that $eS(n,r)e\cong H(r)$, and let
$f_{n,r}:S(n,r)\text{-mod}\to H(r)\text{-mod}$, $V\mapsto eV$, be the exact
Schur functor with left adjoint $h_{n,r}$
([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Let
$L_n(\lambda)$ be the irreducible $S(n,r)$-module for an $\ell$-restricted
$\lambda\vdash r$
([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]), and let
$L_n(\lambda)^1$ be its first level, the sum of the weight spaces
$L_n(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ over the simple roots, which is naturally an
$S(n-1,r-1)$-module. Then

1. $f_{n-1,r-1}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)^1\bigr)=f_{n,r}\bigl(L_n(\lambda)\bigr)
   \bigl\downarrow_{H(r-1)}$ as $H(r-1)$-modules, naturally in the pair
   $(n,r)$;
2. for $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$ one has
   $\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV)$,
   so the functor detects and preserves the relevant Hom spaces and, being
   exact, transfers composition multiplicities of first-level modules;
3. if $\lambda$ is $\ell$-restricted, then the socle of the restriction of
   $L_n(\lambda)^1$ to the Levi subalgebra $U(n-1)$ consists of
   $\ell$-restricted labels.

At $q=1$ (so $\ell=p$ in characteristic $p$; characteristic zero gives
$\ell=\infty$) the specialization $H(r)\to kS_r$ of
([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]])
makes (i)-(iii) statements about $kS_r$-modules and the simple $kS_{r-1}$-modules
of
[[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]].
before.strategy: Complete argument, Brundan 1998 §5.5-5.7 (complete 34-page author manuscript, pp. 30-32) and Kleshchev I §2.12(v), whose citation is replaced by this proof-bearing comparison. (i) Take the permitted stable rank $n=r$ and write the $(1^r)$-weight idempotent of $S(n,r)$; by §3.22 of the source the weight belongs to the level-1 summand, and deleting the last (level) coordinate of the weight identifies it with the $(1^{r-1})$-weight of $S(n-1,r-1)$, while the generators $T_1,\dots,T_{r-2}$ act identically before and after the deletion. Hence both sides are equal as explicit simultaneous weight spaces, naturally in $V$; this uses neither semisimplicity nor an identification of cellular and crystal labels. (ii) Is Brundan's Lemma 5.6(i)-(ii), proved by the adjunction $h\dashv f$ and the submodule $V_{(e)}$; (iii) is Lemma 5.7, whose proof uses the good-node description of the socle and shows that $i\in R^{good}(\lambda)$ implies $\lambda(i)$ is $\ell$-restricted. Composition multiplicities: apply the exact functor $f$ to a composition series of the first-level module; a surviving restricted simple maps to a Hecke simple, a killed simple contributes nothing, and by (ii) the multiplicity of a selected surviving simple is preserved. The $q=1$ specialization is the Hecke/group identification of the batch-20 item. This is the exact replacement for Kleshchev I §2.12(v) as recorded by the SYMR-9 evidence report; Step 3 must keep the weight-idempotent computation explicit.

after.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
after.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).
after.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The nonzero images have restricted labels and are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Every Schur simple $L(\mu)$ is its nonzero cell-form quotient, so the descended symmetric associative form makes $L(\mu)^\circ\cong L(\mu)$ under Schur star. The normalized maps are $\varphi_{ST}(x_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}\in x_\mu H\cap Hx_\nu$ and $m_{TS}=m_{ST}^*$; Schur star is $\varphi_{ST}^*=\varphi_{TS}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The standard coefficient trace satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{uv}q^{\ell(u)}$; its complete generator-block proof is the actual standalone trace construction of [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]. The following proof establishes the restricted-socle conclusion locally over the original field; no quantum-hyperalgebra square-root or unproved classical-specialization premise is used.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $\beta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $\beta_\alpha(aT_i,b)=\beta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $\tau(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q)\beta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_\nu\to M_\mu$, $a=x_\nu h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_\nu m_{TS}=P_\nu m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu\beta_\mu(fa,b)=\tau(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_\nu\beta_\nu(a,f^*b)=\tau(h^*x_\nu m_{TS}k)=P_\nu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k).$$ Cancel the nonzero polynomials only in $A$, then specialize the resulting identity to $F$. The orthogonal sum $\beta=\bigoplus_\alpha\beta_\alpha$ is therefore perfect and satisfies $\beta(sm,m')=\beta(m,s^*m')$ for every actual Schur basis map and hence every $s\in S$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. The last bijection evaluates a map at $e$, with inverse $v\mapsto(se\mapsto sv)$ for $v\in eL$. By [F2], $eL(\mu)$ is nonzero exactly for restricted $\mu$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. The proof does not equate zero form quotients with zero actual module heads. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.2, algebra]


4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

4.2 Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. The length-additive parabolic coset basis makes $H(r)$ free as a LEFT $H(r-1)$-module of rank $r$, so $M_1$ is $r$ copies of $M_0$ as a left lower Schur module. Apply steps 2.2 and 3.2 to $M_0\cong S(n-1,r-1)e_{\rm lower}$: its simple socle labels are exactly the surviving restricted labels. Every simple submodule of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ is a simple submodule of $M_1$, and therefore restricted. At degree zero $M_0=F$, with the unique empty label; at $n=r=1$ this is the convention $S(0,0)=F$. This proves assertion3, without adjoining a square root, using a splitting extension, assuming a quantum-hyperalgebra specialization, or requiring $\lambda_n=0$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]


5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 4.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

The first-level and ordinary-label reconciliation above is the new authored binding repair. The previously accepted source20 cell-form repair and NEW50 ordinary polytabloid construction are unchanged. Actual acceptance requires the repaired current source20/NEW50 supplier carriers after the live writers drain and the same reviewer checks the actual bound interfaces. No further primitive bridge construction is claimed. No identification of cellular and crystal simple labels is used ([[rem-the-crystal-identification-does-not-elementarily-identify-cellular-simple-labels]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prime $p=e=3$, the partitions $(3)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,1,1)$ of $n=3$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,3)$ for $d\ge3$ over any field $F$ of characteristic $3$, with $q=1$ and quantum characteristic $e=3$ (for example $F=\mathbb F_3$).

The specific three-row computation is proved below.

[F3] The exact integral Schur corner/form/radical identity is [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], steps 1.1–5.1. The specific Murphy forms/actions are computed locally from the independent integral Murphy datum and row action ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). The signed conjugate module/form identity is [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. No universal finite-$e$ restricted nonzero criterion is used.

[F4] Group side: the simple $k[S_3]$-modules at $p=3$ are $D^{(3)}$ and $D^{(2,1)}$, indexed by the $3$-regular partitions $(3),(2,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F5] Tabloid model: the permutation module $M^{(2,1)}_k$ over a field $k$ has the three tabloids $v_1,v_2,v_3$ as a basis, where $v_i$ is the tabloid whose singleton second row is $\{i\}$, and $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$; the Specht module $S^{(2,1)}_k\subseteq M^{(2,1)}_k$ has basis $e_t=v_3-v_1$ and $e_u=v_2-v_1$. Moreover $S^{(3)}_k$ is the trivial module and $S^{(1,1,1)}_k$ is the sign module ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]], [[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$. [given, F1]

2.1 Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$, so the quotient is the sign module. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F4], the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

item.title: Generic cyclotomic type-A support is bounded by rank
item.statement:
Let $k$ have characteristic zero, let $\xi\in k^\times$ have infinite
multiplicative order, and fix a finite integral multicharge
$m_1,\ldots,m_\ell$. Write $S=\{m_j:1\le j\le\ell\}$.
Use the arbitrary-base presentations of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]] to define
$H_d^{\deg}$ by $\prod_j(x_1-m_j)=0$ and $H_d^{\xi}$ by
$\prod_j(X_1-\xi^{m_j})=0$.
For $d>0$, every nonzero joint generalized weight in the regular module has
labels $\nu\in\mathbb Z^d$, with eigenvalues $\nu_r$ respectively
$\xi^{\nu_r}$, and
$$\min_{s\in S}|\nu_r-s|\le d-1.$$
Thus both algebras have finite joint spectral decompositions defined over $k$.

Use the directed line $i\to i+1$ on $\mathbb Z$, with $d_i=1$,
$Q_{i,i+1}(u,v)=v-u$, $Q_{i+1,i}(u,v)=u-v$ and $Q_{ij}=1$ for
$|i-j|>1$. Define the rank-$d$ cyclotomic KLR algebra as the direct sum of its
finite-content presentations, with first-strand exponents
$\lambda_i=\#\{j:m_j=i\}$. Every nonzero word idempotent satisfies the same
bound, so this rank algebra is a finite sum of finite-dimensional graded
content algebras. Any interval containing
$[\min S-d+1,\max S+d-1]$ gives exactly the same rank-$d$ algebra;
enlarging it introduces only zero word idempotents. Rank zero is $k$.
At level zero every positive rank is zero. This lemma supplies support and
finite windows; it asserts no Hecke--KLR isomorphism or basis correspondence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The presentations and parameters of the Statement.

[F1] The arbitrary monic cyclotomic Hecke quotients are finite-dimensional by
[[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-bounded-ordered-monomials-span]]. Their mixed and
quadratic relations are those of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]].

[F2] In the KLR presentation, a crossing between distant colors has square
$1$ and interchanges their word idempotents
([[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]).
On any finite color interval, homogeneous cyclotomic content algebras are
finite-dimensional with nilpotent dots
([[lem-cyclotomic-klr-dot-annihilators-and-finite-root-strings]]).

## Proof

1.1 Work over a finite splitting extension for the finitely many minimal polynomials of the commuting polynomial generators in the finite regular module of [F1]. Simultaneous primary decomposition gives joint generalized eigenspaces. On such a weight, the first value is a charge root, because the first cyclotomic polynomial annihilates the module. In the degenerate case connect distinct values differing by $1$; in the nondegenerate case connect distinct nonzero values whose ratio is $\xi$ or $\xi^{-1}$. This defines a graph on the distinct values in each word, with at most $d$ vertices. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a KLR word, form the induced line graph on its distinct colors. If a component contains no charge, move its first occurrence left across all earlier letters. These letters lie in other components, so their color differences exceed $1$; [F2] makes every crossing invertible. The resulting word idempotent is nonzero if the original was, but its first color has exponent zero, so the cyclotomic relation kills it. This contradiction shows that each component contains a charge. A component with at most $d$ vertices is an interval, and every color has distance at most $d-1$ from a charge in that component. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The mixed relations give intertwiners $\theta_r=s_r(x_r-x_{r+1})+1$ and $\Theta_r=T_r(1-X_rX_{r+1}^{-1})+1-\xi$. Direct multiplication gives $\theta_r^2=1-(x_r-x_{r+1})^2$ and $\Theta_r^2=(1-\xi X_{r+1}X_r^{-1})(1-\xi X_rX_{r+1}^{-1})$; they interchange the two polynomial generators and commute with the others. For example $s_r(x_r-x_{r+1})=-(x_r-x_{r+1})s_r-2$, which yields the first square identity; the second follows by inserting $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$ and $T_rX_rT_r=\xi X_{r+1}$. Between values in different graph components these squares have nonzero constant terms, hence are invertible on the generalized weight space. Each intertwiner therefore gives an isomorphism onto the swapped generalized weight space. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose a component contains no charge root. Its earliest occurrence in the word can be moved to the first position by the invertible swaps of step 2.1: every preceding value belongs to a different component. The resulting nonzero weight space has an uncharged first value, contradicting the first cyclotomic relation. Consequently each component contains a charge root. A simple path from that root to any vertex has length at most $d-1$, so the value is an integer within $d-1$ of an integral charge, respectively a power $\xi^a$ with $|a-m_j|\le d-1$. Infinite order of $\xi$ makes the integer labels unique. All spectral values therefore belong to $k$, and their polynomial primary projectors descend to $k$ by the Chinese remainder identity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Only finitely many words satisfy this bound. In every content presentation the generators and relations use only colors already present in that content, so replacing the full line by a finite interval containing the bound changes none of these presentations. All omitted contents have zero word idempotents by step 1.2. On the finite interval [F2] supplies finite-dimensionality and nilpotent dots, and the finite sum is finite-dimensional. This identifies the full rank algebra with each sufficiently large finite window, including compatibility of larger windows on the same generators. At level zero the first exponent is always zero, killing every positive-rank word; the Hecke polynomial is $1$ and gives the same zero quotient. Rank zero is the ground field by definition. No basis correspondence or Hecke--KLR inverse map has been used. [step 3.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, given] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The characteristic-zero field, finite integer interval, multiset, presentations, completions and specified series in the Statement.

[F1] The native KLR presentation in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] has the two equal-color dot moves for $\tau$, the quadratic polynomial $Q$, and the reversed-word braid numerator $[Q(u,v)-Q(w,v)]/(w-u)$. Replacing $\tau$ by $-\psi$ gives $\psi u-v\psi=-1$, $\psi v-u\psi=1$, and $\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1-\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2=[Q(u,v)-Q(w,v)]/(w-u)$ on colors $(a,b,a)$.

[F2] The degenerate affine Hecke generator presentation of [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]] over $\mathbb C$ has the relations listed in the Statement; here that presentation defines the algebra over $k$, and its basis and faithful action are proved below. The generators $s_r$ permute positions; the distinct notation $\sigma_r$ below means actual permutation operators on polynomial or formal coefficient functions.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and conventions of the Statement, and [F1]–[F2].

1.1 The coefficient completions. A symmetric polynomial in the commuting $x$ is central: the mixed relation gives $s_rf=(\sigma_rf)s_r-(f-\sigma_rf)/(x_r-x_{r+1})$, first on monomials by induction, then on polynomials. A symmetric $f$ has zero correction. The fiber of the elementary symmetric polynomials over their values on $\beta$ consists exactly of the ordered permutations of $\beta$: the coordinates are roots with multiplicities of $\prod_{a\in\beta}(t-a)$. Its radical is the intersection of the finitely many corresponding maximal ideals, by the polynomial factorization and the fact that every coordinate satisfies this monic polynomial. The elementary-symmetric ideal and this radical have cofinal powers, since the fiber is finite dimensional and its radical nilpotent. Chinese remainders and completion therefore give $\mathcal B_\beta$ with local coordinates $x_r-\nu_r$. On the KLR side symmetric dot polynomials are central by [F1], and the same argument at the all-zero fiber shows that its coefficient completion is $\mathcal B_\beta$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Invertible tables. If $a\ne b$ the integer $a-b$ is a nonzero unit in $k$, so $z^{-1}$ exists as a formal geometric series. In the backward case $a=b+1$, $q=z^{-1}$ has constant $1$. In the other unequal cases $q=1-z^{-1}$ has constant $1-(a-b)^{-1}$, which could vanish only when $a-b=1$, already excluded. Equal colors give constant $1$. For unequal colors $p_{ba}(v,u)=-p_{ab}(u,v)$. Direct multiplication gives $q_{ab}(u,v)q_{ba}(v,u)=1-z^{-2}$ on nonadjacent colors; on a forward arrow it gives $-(z-1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(v-u)$ since $z=-1+u-v$; on a backward arrow it gives $(z+1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(u-v)$ since $z=1+u-v$. Thus $Q_{ab}q_{ab}\sigma(q_{ba})=1-p_{ab}^2$ in all unequal cases, with no division by a nonunit left unresolved. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 A concrete KLR action. On $\mathcal B_\beta$, dots multiply and idempotents project. Define $E_r=(\sigma_r-1)/(y_r-y_{r+1})$ on equal adjacent colors. The numerator is divisible by the denominator for polynomials and formal series, so $E_r$ preserves the coefficient algebra. For unequal source colors $(a,b)$ define $\psi_r(fe(\nu))=c_{ab}(y_r,y_{r+1})\sigma_r(f)e(s_r\nu)$, where $c_{ab}(u,v)=v-u$ if $a=b+1$ and $c_{ab}(u,v)=1$ otherwise. These explicit operators prove the local relations in the following five cases. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Quadratic and dot moves. Write $\delta=u-v$. On equal colors $E^2=0$, since $E(f)$ is invariant under $\sigma$, and $Eu-vE=-1$, $Ev-uE=1$ follow by expanding the numerator. On unequal colors the dot moves are permutation identities and $\psi^2=c_{ba}(u,v)c_{ab}(v,u)=Q_{ab}(u,v)$. Indeed these products are $v-u$ on a forward arrow, $u-v$ on a backward arrow, and $1$ off edges. Disjoint crossings commute because their variables and their two-color factors are disjoint. Idempotent moves and commutative dot relations hold by construction. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Three distinct colors. Put $u=y_1,v=y_2,w=y_3$, $s=\sigma_1,t=\sigma_2$, $\rho=sts=tst$, $L=\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1$, $M=\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2$. On a source $(a,b,c)$ with all colors distinct, direct consecutive application of step 3.1 gives both $L(f)$ and $M(f)$ equal to $c_{bc}(u,v)c_{ac}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)$ in the $(c,b,a)$ summand. The three pair factors commute. Hence $L=M$ for every edge pattern among three distinct integer colors. [step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra]

6.1 Exactly the first two equal. On $(a,a,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,v)c_{ab}(u,w)$. Consecutive application gives $L(f)=h\,stE_1(f)$ and $M(f)=E_2(h\,stf)$. The polynomial $h$ is symmetric in $v,w$, including the backward case $h=(v-u)(w-u)$, so the product rule $E_2(hg)=E_2(h)g+t(h)E_2(g)$ gives $M(f)=hE_2stf$. Finally $E_2st=stE_1$: both sides equal $(\rho-st)/(v-w)$, with the denominator transformed when the permutation lies to its left. Thus $L=M$. [step 5.1, step 3.1, algebra]

7.1 Exactly the last two equal. On $(a,b,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)$. The two words give $L(f)=E_1(h\,tsf)$ and $M(f)=h\,tsE_2(f)$. Here $h$ is symmetric in $u,v$, including $h=(w-u)(w-v)$ when $a=b+1$. The product rule gives $L(f)=hE_1tsf$. The identity $E_1ts=tsE_2=(\rho-ts)/(u-v)$ now yields $L=M$. This explicitly checks the second repeated-neighbor pattern. [step 6.1, step 3.1, algebra]

8.1 Equal outer colors. On $(a,b,a)$, $a\ne b$, full expansion of the single middle divided difference gives $L(f)=c_{ba}(u,v)[c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)-c_{ab}(v,u)f]/(u-w)$ and $M(f)=c_{ab}(v,w)[c_{ba}(u,v)\rho(f)-c_{ba}(w,v)f]/(u-w)$. The $\rho(f)$ terms cancel, and step 4.1 gives $(L-M)(f)=[Q_{ab}(w,v)-Q_{ab}(u,v)]f/(u-w)$. Thus the correction is $+1$ for $a\to b$, $-1$ for $a\leftarrow b$, and zero off edges. The displayed expressions have removable denominators because their original numerators come from divided differences; the final quotient is a polynomial. [step 7.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

9.1 All three equal. For $\Delta=(u-v)(u-w)(v-w)$, expand the three factors $E=(\sigma-1)/(\text{dot difference})$ in either order. Moving permutations to the right gives the complete identity $E_1E_2E_1=E_2E_1E_2=(\rho-st-ts+s+t-1)/\Delta$. For example the $\rho$ coefficient is $1/\Delta$, the $st$ and $ts$ coefficients are $-1/\Delta$, the $s,t$ coefficients are $1/\Delta$, and the identity coefficient is $-1/\Delta$. Both sides preserve formal series by their original divided-difference formulas, so this rational equality proves their equality without inverting dots in the algebra. This supplies the all-equal case omitted in the cited source. [step 8.1, step 3.1, algebra]

10.1 Faithfulness for the KLR action. Moving dots to the right using step 4.1, and replacing repeated crossings and braid differences using steps 5.1–9.1, spans the presented KLR algebra by $\psi_w f(y)e(\nu)$ for fixed reduced words $w$. Termination uses crossing length: every quadratic reduction or braid correction has smaller length; reduced words for a permutation are connected by the elementary symmetric-group braid moves. In the rational-function action each $\psi_w$ has leading term a nonzero coefficient times $w$, and all other terms have smaller permutation length. Distinct permutations of variables are linearly independent over the rational-function field: a shortest putative relation, evaluated on $fg$ minus one selected automorphism's value on $g$ times its evaluation on $f$, gives a shorter nonzero relation. Hence these spanning monomials are independent. The same triangular argument over fractions of formal series proves faithfulness of the completed action, whose elements are the finite sum over $w,\nu$ with formal coefficient $f$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

11.1 Why formal extension is legitimate. There are finitely many $w,\nu$, and each basis vector $\psi_we(\nu)$ has a finite crossing degree. Symmetric positive-degree dots form a central ideal with powers cofinal with dot-degree powers in each coefficient algebra by step 1.1. The PBW module just proved is consequently finite free over its right coefficient algebra and completes coefficientwise. Multiplication extends continuously: moving a formal coefficient through a crossing uses a variable permutation or one divided difference, decreasing its order by at most one, so any finite product has a uniform finite order loss. The displayed completed PBW expansion is therefore the actual central completion, rather than an additional relation imposed on $R_\beta$. [step 1.1, step 10.1, algebra]

12.1 The common degenerate Hecke operator. In the fraction algebra set $Z_r=x_r-x_{r+1}$ and $S_r=(1+Z_r^{-1})\sigma_r-Z_r^{-1}$. On an unequal source component the diagonal term is $-z^{-1}f$, while its crossing coefficient on the target component is $1+(b-a+u-v)^{-1}$. On equal colors this operator is $\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$ and preserves formal series. Thus $S_r$ acts on $\mathcal B_\beta$ in every case. All identities in the next two steps are computed in the fraction algebra and then hold for these regular operators. This use of auxiliary fractions does not assert that a dot difference is invertible in the completion or its quotients. [step 11.1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

13.1 Hecke quadratic and mixed identities. Let $A=Z_r^{-1}$; then $\sigma_r(A)=-A$. Expanding $S_r^2$ gives identity coefficient $(1+A)(1-A)+A^2=1$ and crossing coefficient $(1+A)A-A(1+A)=0$. Thus $S_r^2=1$, including equal colors. In $S_rx_{r+1}-x_rS_r$ the crossing terms cancel and the diagonal term is $A(x_r-x_{r+1})=1$. Disjoint $S_r$ commute, and dots outside the pair commute with $S_r$. These are precisely the quadratic, mixed and far-commuting relations of [F2]. [F2, step 12.1, algebra]

14.1 Complete Hecke braid coefficients. In spectral variables put $Z=x_1-x_2$, $U=x_2-x_3$, $V=Z+U$, $A=Z^{-1}$, $B=U^{-1}$, $C=V^{-1}$. Both products $S_1S_2S_1$ and $S_2S_1S_2$ have coefficients, in permutation order $(1,s,t,st,ts,\rho)$, equal to $(-C-ABC,\ (1+A)BC,\ (1+B)AC,\ -B(1+A)(1+C),\ -A(1+B)(1+C),\ (1+A)(1+B)(1+C))$. To verify the reductions, multiply using $(f\sigma)(g\eta)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\eta$, $s(A)=-A$, $s(B)=C$, $t(B)=-B$, $t(A)=C$, and $AB=C(A+B)$. For example the raw $s$ coefficient in the first word is $A(1+A)(B-C)=(1+A)BC$; its raw identity coefficient is $-(1-A^2)C-A^2B=-C-ABC$. Interchanging $A,B$ and $s,t$ gives the second word's identical six coefficients. [step 13.1, step 12.1, algebra]

15.1 All five reverse braid cases. Step 14.1 is a rational identity in independent spectral variables, before assigning colors. Substitute $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(a+u,b+v,c+w)$ on each source component and apply the color-permuting operators. It proves the full Hecke braid separately on $(a,b,c)$ with all distinct, $(a,a,b)$, $(a,b,b)$, $(a,b,a)$ and $(a,a,a)$, because each is the restriction of the same six-coefficient identity and every $S_r$ preserves $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 12.1. Even when a displayed spectral denominator has zero constant, cancellation occurs in the original regular operators, and injectivity into fractions preserves the equality. Thus the all-equal reverse case also has a complete coefficient computation. [step 12.1, step 14.1, algebra]

16.1 Faithfulness for the Hecke action. The mixed relation moves polynomials to the right of $s$-words and the exact symmetric-group relations reduce each word to $s_w$, so $H_n^{\mathrm{dg}}$ is spanned by $s_wf(x)$. In the action of steps 12.1–15.1 its leading permutation coefficient is the product of nonzero rational factors $1+Z^{-1}$ along a reduced word. All lower terms have shorter permutation length. The shortest-relation argument of step 10.1 proves independence and therefore the affine Hecke PBW basis. Completing at the central ideal of step 1.1 gives the finite coefficientwise PBW module $\sum_{w,\nu}s_w k[\![y]\!]e(\nu)$; its operator action remains faithful by the same argument over formal fractions. The coefficients $1+Z^{-1}$ need only be nonzero in that field, not units in the coefficient ring. [F2, step 1.1, step 10.1, step 13.1, step 15.1, algebra]

17.1 Comparing the explicit tables. On an unequal source $(a,b)$, $S_r+p_{ab}$ has only the crossing term. Its target coefficient is $1+\zeta^{-1}$, where $\zeta=b-a+u-v$. Right multiplication by $q_{ab}^{-1}$ substitutes $(v,u)$ on that target. If $a\to b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=1+\zeta^{-1}$, giving coefficient $1$; if $a\leftarrow b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=-\zeta^{-1}$ and $\zeta=-1+u-v$, giving coefficient $-(\zeta+1)=v-u$; off edges the quotient is again $1$. On equal colors $S_r=\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$, and $(S_r+1)(1+v-u)^{-1}=(\sigma_r-1)/(u-v)=E_r$ by moving the inverse through $\sigma_r$. Thus $(S_r+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ in the faithful action. Equivalently $\psi_rq-p=S_r$. [step 16.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 12.1, algebra]

18.1 Homomorphisms in both directions. Faithfulness in steps 10.1–11.1 and 16.1 transfers the concrete equalities to the completed presented algebras. Step 17.1 identifies the forward images with the operators checked in steps 4.1–9.1, so all KLR relations hold in $\widehat H_\beta^{\mathrm{dg}}$. It identifies the reverse images with the operators checked in steps 13.1–15.1, so all Hecke relations hold in $\widehat R_\beta$. The coefficient-algebra maps identify the central completion topologies: the symmetric ideal vanishing at the spectral multiset and the all-zero dot ideal have cofinal powers on $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 1.1. Therefore the maps extend continuously to the stated completions. This proves both directions locally rather than importing a cyclic finite-$e$ theorem. [step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 11.1, step 13.1, step 15.1, step 16.1, step 17.1, construct]

19.1 Inverse composites and uniformity. The coefficient maps fix every $e(\nu)$ and invert $y_r=x_r-\nu_r$ componentwise. The crossing composites are $(\psi_rq-p+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ and $((s_r+p)q^{-1})q-p=s_r$, with the same right multiplication order. Hence each composite is the identity on its generators, coefficient series and completion. None of $p,q,c$ depends on the rank, multiset, interval endpoints, level or cyclotomic charge, so enlarging an interval preserves every formula on the old tuples. Nilpotent dots permit finite evaluation of series, and every proved identity survives a quotient. Rank zero has coefficient algebra $k$ and both maps are the identity; empty positive-rank sectors have zero algebra. No assertion about cyclotomic support, based Grothendieck classes or Specht modules is needed for this local comparison. [step 18.1, algebra] ∎
